questiontext.text:
Two loudspeakers driven in phase sit 4.0 cm apart and emit sound of wavelength 1.2 cm toward a wall 60 cm away.

What is the spacing between adjacent bright fringes along the wall, in cm? (Enter a number only.)

generalfeedback.text:
Δy = λL/d = (1.2 cm)(60 cm)/(4.0 cm) = 18 cm.

The fringe spacing grows with the wavelength and with the distance to the wall, and shrinks as the sources are moved apart. Units check: cm × cm ÷ cm = cm, a length, as it must be.

feedback.text: You put the source spacing d in the numerator. In Δy = λL/d, moving the sources farther apart should pack the fringes closer together — so d belongs underneath.
You swapped the roles of L and d. Which of the two is the distance to the wall, and where does it sit in Δy = λL/d?
You divided the distance to the wall by the source spacing but left the wavelength out. Δy scales with λ as well — a longer wavelength spreads the fringes.
Use Δy = λL/d: wavelength times the distance to the wall, divided by the separation of the sources. Keep every length in centimetres and the answer comes out in centimetres.

name.text: KO5-B · Bright or dark at a point

questiontext.text:
Two sources emit waves in phase. A point Q is 6.0 m from one source and 7.0 m from the other. The wavelength is 0.40 m.

Is Q a point of constructive or destructive interference?

generalfeedback.text:
Destructive — Q is dark.

The path difference is Δr = 7.0 m − 6.0 m = 1.0 m. In wavelengths that is 1.0 m ÷ 0.40 m = 2.5 — a half-integer. Written as (m + ½)λ with m = 2, so the second wave arrives exactly half a cycle behind: crest meets trough and they cancel.

Only the leftover fraction of a wavelength matters: 0.5λ, 1.5λ and 2.5λ all give complete cancellation; whole numbers of wavelengths give a maximum.

incorrectfeedback.text: Find the path difference, divide by the wavelength, and look at the leftover fraction: a whole number is a maximum, a half is a cancellation.

answer.text: Destructive — the waves arrive exactly out of step, so Q is dark

feedback.text: Correct — the path difference is 2.5 wavelengths, a half-integer.

answer.text: Constructive — the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, so Q is bright

feedback.text: Work out the path difference in metres, then divide by 0.40 m. Is the result a whole number, or does it land halfway between two whole numbers?

answer.text: Neither — it falls halfway between a bright point and a dark point

feedback.text: A path difference of exactly 2.5 wavelengths is not an in-between case: it is one of the two extremes. Which one happens when the waves are a half-cycle apart?

answer.text: Cannot tell without knowing how far Q is from a screen

feedback.text: Whether a given point is bright or dark depends only on the two path lengths to it and the wavelength — not on any screen. You already have all three numbers.
